title: Bioepoxy matrices reinforced with wheat straw-derived nanobiochar (NBC) or cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs)
abstract: Abstract Bioepoxy resins offer a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based polymers; however, their intrinsic brittleness restricts their use in structural applications. This study investigates the reinforcing effects of nanobiochar (NBC) and cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) on the mechanical and thermal properties of bioepoxy composites, with an aim of enhancing fracture toughness. Untreated nanoparticles were pre-dispersed in methanol to improve dispersion prior to incorporation into the bioepoxy. Characterisation included Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy to confirm chemical integrity, Dynamic Light Scattering for particle size distribution, Brunauer‐Emmett‐Teller analysis for surface area, and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) for fracture surface morphology. Rheological analysis assessed dispersion quality, while mechanical performance was evaluated through tensile tests and single-edge notch bending for fracture toughness. Viscoelastic behaviour and glass transition temperature were examined via Dynamic Mechanical Analysis. NBC consistently outperformed CNCs in reinforcing the bioepoxy. At 5 wt%, CNCs increased Young’s modulus by 13.6% (3.5 ± 0.2 GPa), however, agglomeration at higher loadings reduced effectiveness. NBC (10 wt%) achieved a 24.2% increase in Young’s modulus (3.8 ± 0.3 GPa) and improved ultimate tensile strength by 9.2% (71 ± 2 MPa) at 3 wt%. Fracture tests showed that CNCs improved mode I fracture toughness by 37.2% at 3 wt% (110 ± 11 J m −2 ), whereas NBC produced a 72.7% increase at 7 wt% (138 ± 5 J m −2 ). SEM analysis revealed mechanisms such as crack pinning and deflection, although voids and agglomerates limited CNC performance. Thermal analysis showed an increase in Tg with nanoparticle addition, reaching 69.1 ± 0.1 °C for NBC at 7 wt% (5.3% increase). Overall, NBC significantly improved stiffness, strength, fracture toughness, and thermal stability, demonstrating its potential as a high performance, sustainable nanofiller for bioepoxy composites.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The United Nations has established the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), to guide global efforts toward a more sustainable and equitable future. SDG 12 aim of ensuring sustainable consumption and production patterns, promoting resource efficiency, waste reduction, and sustainable practices is of particular relevance to material science researchers (Venkatachalam et al.  42 ; United Nations  41 ; Grant et al.  14 ). In the field of composite materials, bioepoxy is a versatile matrix which is used as a binding agent for fibres in fibre-reinforced polymer composites (FRPCs) (Liu et al.  27 ). These composites are used across a wide range of sectors, from renewable energy applications such as wind turbine blades to advanced components in the aerospace and automotive industries. To further enhance the properties of epoxy-based FRPCs, several high-performance nanoparticles such as Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs), Graphene Nanoplatelets (GNPs), Boron Nitride Nanotubes (BNNTs), and Boron Nitride Nanosheets (BNNS) have been incorporated to improve their mechanical, thermal, and electrical properties. However, the high cost and environmentally unsustainable production methods counter their practical advantages (Domun et al.  10 ). Therefore, recent research has focused on finding more sustainable, environmentally friendly and cost-effective alternatives.

Cellulose Nanocrystals (CNCs) represent a major advancement in sustainable materials science, serving as highly effective reinforcing fillers for polymer matrices, due to their renewability, biodegradability, and tuneable surface chemistry (Aziz et al.  3 ). Their appeal lies in their renewable nature, low density, and exceptional mechanical properties, including a high Young’s modulus and tensile strength, often surpassing those of many traditional fillers. This superior mechanical performance arises from their high crystallinity and nanoscale dimensions, which lead to a high surface area. This large surface area facilitates strong interfacial adhesion, allowing for efficient stress transfer and the formation of a stiff, load-bearing percolation network at low filler loadings. Furthermore, the numerous surface hydroxy groups allow for diverse chemical modifications, making the surface chemistry highly tuneable and improving dispersion and compatibility across a wide range of polymer systems. These combined attributes make nanocellulose and CNCs ideal candidates for developing lightweight, high-performance, and environmentally friendly materials for applications in aerospace, packaging, and biomedicine (Trinh and Mekonnen  40 ). Zheng et al. ( 47 ) reported that CNCs significantly improved thermal stability and adhesion when surface-modified with phenolic and acrylic resins; however, their brittleness and poor dispersion at higher loadings remained significant limitations. Their findings demonstrated CNCs’ ability to enhance modulus and adhesive properties, even though mechanical gains plateau beyond 5 wt% due to agglomeration and stress concentration effects. Haq et al. ( 17 ) highlighted CNC’s biodegradability and renewability as key advantages for sustainable composites and noting that acid hydrolysis produces chemical effluents requiring treatment. They identified CNCs as promising materials for circular economy applications and emphasise the need for more environmentally responsible processing methods. A 29.5% increase in modulus and a 38.7% increase in strength were achieved when 5 wt% CNCs were added to an epoxy matrix. Nascimento et al. ( 33 ) reported a 26.4% increase in modulus but a 53% decrease in Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) was observed when 7 vol% CNCs were added to an epoxy matrix. The decline in strength was attributed due to stress concentrations arising at the ends of the rod-like CNCs.

Biobased nanoparticles have emerged as promising alternatives to the traditional nanoparticles. CNCs and NBC are biobased nanoparticles produced from natural biomass, whereas GNPs, CNTs, BNPs, and BNNs are synthetic nanoparticles derived from non-renewable sources. However, CNCs and biochar (BC) differ fundamentally in their production methods and reinforcement mechanism. CNCs are produced through hydrolysis of cellulose with strong acids. In contrast, biochar is produced via thermal methods such as pyrolysis, torrefaction, carbonisation, and gasification, which expose waste biomass to intense heat in the absence of oxygen, without the need for harsh chemicals. This environmentally friendly process yields a material with high porosity, which, when added to a polymer, enhances bonding primarily through mechanical interlocking as the polymer infiltrates the porous structure (Amusat et al.  1 ; Mensah et al.  31 ).

The morphology of biochar depends on the source material and the conditions used in synthesis. Bartoli et al. ( 5 ) synthesised biochar from olive pruning using pyrolysis at varying temperatures and heating rates to optimise its morphology for improving properties of a bioepoxy polymer matrix. Biochar produced at 400 °C with a heating rate (HR) of 50 °C/min enhanced ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and Young’s modulus by 65% and 35%, respectively. Other biochar produced at the same high treatment temperature (HTT) with varying heating rates improved maximum elongation by up to 29% compared to the neat resin. At 600 °C, biochar with HRs of 5 °C/min and 15 °C/min increased Young’s modulus and UTS by up to 33% and 70%, respectively. The variations in properties were attributed to biochar morphology. Notably, biochar produced at 1000 °C achieved the highest maximum elongation, improving it by up to 54% compared to the neat resin (Bartoli et al.  5 ).

In another study, Bartoli et al. ( 4 ), used commercially available micro sized biochar to improve the properties of an epoxy matrix. They found that biochar derived from wheat straw pellet (WSP) at 550 °C doubled the Young’s modulus and UTS compared to the neat epoxy, while Miscanthus-derived biochar increased the elongation by 40%. Scavuzzo et al. ( 37 ) also used the commercially available Miscanthus-derived biochar to improve the mechanical and electromagnetic properties of epoxy composites. They annealed the biochar at 800 °C and produced a hybrid iron-rich filler to fine-tune the surface and bulk properties. Their key finding was that hybrid composites containing 20 wt% biochar exhibited a 27% increase in Young’s modulus over the neat epoxy resin. Further increases in biochar weight content led to agglomeration and a decrease in performance. In addition, biochar-epoxy composites demonstrated enhanced conductivity at higher filler loadings, making them suitable for high-frequency applications such as antennas, and other electromagnetic components.

Biochar has shown superior mechanical properties compared to the more expensive carbon nanotubes in epoxy matrices (Khan et al.  24 ). The enhanced UTS and toughness compared to CNTs was attributed to the large surface area of the biochar, thus increasing the stress transfer.

The previous studies utilised micro-sized biochar to improve the properties of polymer matrices. Reducing the size of biochar to the nanoscale can benefit from the interphase phenomena that occur in polymer nanocomposites. When filler particles with diameter (D) smaller than twice the radius of gyration (Rg) of the polymer chain (2Rg/D > 1) are added to a polymer matrix, the polymer chains are adsorbed onto the particle’s surface. As a result of this adsorption, loop structures are formed around the particles, which entangle with neighbouring polymer chains, restricting the movement of the polymer chains. Consequently, the free volume between the polymer chains decreases and the packing density increases (Grant 2025). This leads to an interphase region, extending a few nanometres from the particle surface, which has properties that are between the polymer and particle. This interphase region increases the properties of nanocomposites by replacing regions of the weaker polymer matrix with a stronger interphase material (Huang et al.  19 ; Grant et al.  14 ). Nanobiochar (NBC) can be made using a variety of methods including ball milling (Naghdi et al.  32 ), sonication (Sajjadi et al.  36 ), centrifugation (Lian et al.  25 ), and hydrothermal synthesis (Guo et al.  15 ). Among all these methods, ball milling stands out as an inexpensive, and reproducible method which is more energy efficient compared to centrifugation and sonication and does not require the use of chemicals like hydrothermal synthesis (Naghdi et al.  32 ).

Ball milling reduces particle size through a combination of impact and attrition when steel balls collide with particles inside a rotating mill. These repeated mechanical stresses fracture the material into smaller and smaller particles. Additionally, the balls roll over each other with the particles in the middle causing further grinding through friction and shear forces (Lyu et al.  28 ). Although ball milling can achieve particle sizes in the nanometre range, there are issues with agglomeration of particles. Naghdi et al. ( 32 ) found that conditioning biochar at − 80 °C prior to ball milling reduced agglomeration, achieving a particle size of 60 nm compared to 102.5 nm when conditioned at − 20 °C and 212.4 nm without pre-conditioning.

Currently, NBC is extensively used for soil improvement due to their large surface area. It has been found to improve soil fertility, act as carbon capture agent, enhance water retention, and improve plant growth and crop yields (Brar et al.  7 ). NBC has also been used for targeted cancer therapy (Iannazzo et al.  20 ), and sensing applications (Espro et al.  13 ). However, relatively little research has examined how NBC influences the viscoelastic and mechanical properties of polymer matrices.

Mayakrishnan et al. ( 29 ) prepared biochar with an average particle size of 80 nm using ball milling to enhance the properties of thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) mulching films. The tensile and tear strengths of the films were increased by 50% and 46%, respectively. At a loading of 10 wt% NBC, the maximum penetration resistance and dart impact strength reached 26.7 N and 279 g. This was attributed to matrix toughening effects and crack propagation resistance. The Burst strength increased from 78.2 to 94.5 kPa.

Understanding fracture properties is crucial in the development of structural composite because these properties dictate the material’s resistance to damage and catastrophic failure. Unlike ductile metals that deform before breaking, composites are brittle and prone to sudden failure once a crack forms. A higher delamination fracture toughness enables the composite to better resist crack propagation caused by impacts, drilled holes, or internal flaws. This resistance is vital, as it prevents minor, often unseen damage from rapidly escalating into a sudden, catastrophic failure, thereby ensuring the structure’s long-term safety and reliability. Semaan et al. ( 38 ) investigated the fracture properties of CNC/epoxy composites and reported an 11% improvement at 2 wt% CNC loading.

The work reported here focuses on reducing the size of commercially available WSP biochar, produced by pyrolysis at 550 °C, down to the nanoscale using cryogenic ball milling at − 80 °C. The resulting NBC is then incorporated into a bioepoxy matrix. This commercial biochar was chosen as it achieved the highest improvement in tensile properties as reported by Bartoli et al. ( 4 ). In their work, they compared commercial biochar materials that were pyrolysed at different temperatures.

Cellulose-based composites have been shown to enhance biodegradability and environmental performance (Chen et al.  8 ; Aziz et al.  3 ), while biochar-based fillers may provide carbon sequestration benefits, lowering the overall carbon footprint of composites (Aziz et al.  2 ; Chen et al.  8 ). Although a detailed life-cycle assessment was beyond the scope of this study, these findings underscore the environmental benefits of bio-based nanofillers and provide a strong foundation for future research on quantitative sustainability metrics.

Bioepoxy resins are increasingly adopted as sustainable alternatives to petroleum-based polymers; however, their inherent brittleness and low fracture toughness severely limit their use in structural applications. Conventional approaches to enhance epoxy performance rely on CNTs, GNPs, and other high-performance nanofillers, which, despite improving mechanical properties, are costly and environmentally burdensome due to energy-intensive and chemical-heavy production processes. This creates a critical need for eco-friendly, cost-effective reinforcement strategies that align with global sustainability goals.

CNCs and NBC have emerged as promising bio-based nanofillers due to their renewability and potential to improve the mechanical and thermal properties of polymer matrices. CNCs offer high stiffness and biodegradability, while NBC provides a porous structure and amphiphilic surface chemistry conducive to strong interface and interphase bonding. However most existing literature focuses primarily on CNC/epoxy systems, with limited attention given to NBC, particularly at the nanoscale. Furthermore, comparative studies evaluating the mechanical, fracture, and viscoelastic performance of CNCs and NBC in bioepoxy matrices are scarce. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no studies have been conducted on the fracture properties of polymer composites incorporating nanosized biochar. This knowledge gap limits the development of optimized bio-based composites for high-performance applications.

This work aims to conduct a comparative study of sustainable bioepoxy matrices modified with CNC and NBC particles, systematically investigating their effects on tensile properties, fracture toughness, rheology, thermal and viscoelastic behaviour. By benchmarking against neat bioepoxy and linking performance to sustainability considerations, the study seeks to determine which nanofiller and at what loading provides superior reinforcement and processing advantages. The finding will also offer design guidelines for next-generation bio-based composites that meet both technical and environmental requirements.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs: The selection of nanofiller loadings, fracture toughness testing, and rheological characterization in this study was guided by prior research on epoxy nanocomposites (Domun et al.  11 ; Trinh and Mekonnen  40 ). CNC loadings (1–7 wt%) were chosen based on Trinh and Mekonnen’s findings, who reported substantial improvements in stiffness and strength at 2.5–5 wt% CNC, followed a decline in performance at higher concentrations due to agglomeration. This range allowed us to capture the optimal reinforcement window while assessing the onset of agglomeration effects. We note that limited studies exist on NBC, so its loadings were initially mirrored from those commonly used for CNC (1–7 wt%) to enable a direct comparison. After this baseline, NBC loadings were progressively increased up to 15 wt%, until a decline in mechanical and viscoelastic properties was observed, indicating the onset of agglomeration. This approach ensured that the optimal reinforcement window and the threshold for performance deterioration were identified.

Similarly, Domun et al.  11  utilised a SENB geometry to evaluate mode I fracture toughness as it provides mode I fracture toughness data for brittle epoxy systems, consistent with ASTM D5045 standards. Rheological and dynamic mechanical analyses were included to evaluate dispersion quality and viscoelastic behaviour, which are critical for processing and long-term performance. These parameters offer insight into how nanofiller morphology and dispersion influence mechanical, fracture, and viscoelastic properties.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Biochar produced by the pyrolysis of wheat straw pellets (WSP) at 550 °C was supplied by the UK Biochar Research Centre (UKBRC) (Edinburgh, Scotland). Spray-dried CNC produced by acid hydrolysis of wood pulp with a particle size of 150 nm was supplied by Celluforce (Quebec, Canada). Analytical grade methanol (≥ 99.9%), acetone (≥ 99.5%), and toluene (≥ 99.5%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (Dorset, United Kingdom). All chemicals were used as received without further purification. Both the IB2 bioepoxy resin system and the Easy-Lease release agent were supplied by Easy Composites UK (Stoke-on-Trent, United Kingdom). The IB2 resin, which exhibits a density of 1.16 g/cm 3 , is notable for utilizing epichlorohydrin synthesized from glycerol derived from waste cooking oil, fats, vegetable oils (such as canola), and biodiesel by-products. This composition offers a renewable alternative to conventional petroleum-based epoxies.

sections.heading: Production of NBC
paragraphs: NBC was prepared according to the procedure reported by Naghdi et al. ( 32 ). WSP biochar was initially balled-milled for 15 min using 15 × 10 mm stainless steel balls. The balled milled BC (10 g) was then conditioned at − 78.5 °C for 24 h, then milled into NBC using a Retsch PM100 planetary ball mill (Retsch GmbH, Germany). The milling was performed at 575 rpm for 100 min in a 500 ml stainless steel jar containing 800 × 2.4 mm stainless steel balls, with a total weight of 45 g.

sections.heading: Particle size distribution of NBC
paragraphs: The particle size distribution of NBC was determined by Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) using a Zetasizer Nano S instrument (Malvern Panalytical, Malvern, UK). NBC (1 mg) was dispersed in distilled water (200 ml) containing 1 wt% methanol using a magnetic stirrer at room temperature for 24 h, then homogenised for 2 min at 19,00 rpm using a homogeniser. Three different samples were tested, and the average was taken.

sections.heading: Surface area measurements
paragraphs: BET specific surface areas were measured via N 2  adsorption isotherms obtained at 77 K using a BEL Sorption Max instrument. A relative pressure ranging from 0.05 to 1 was applied. Prior to analysis, samples were left in a vacuum oven for 24 h at 100 °C. Subsequent measurement involved assessing the amount of N 2  gas adsorbed onto a known sample quantity as a function of relative pressure. The derived isotherm was then analysed using the BET equation to calculate the amount of N 2  corresponding to a complete monolayer on the external and accessible internal pore surfaces of the sample. Three samples were tested, and the average was taken.

sections.heading: Dispersion in different solvents
paragraphs: The dispersion stability of NBC in distilled water, methanol, acetone, and toluene was studied. These solvents were chosen to test a wide range of polarities, with distilled water being the most polar, and toluene the least. NBC (0.5 g) and CNC (0.5 g) were dispersed in 100 ml of the respective solvents using an ultrasonic bath for 1 h, then homogenised at 19,000 rpm for 2 min using a D-130 high speed homogeniser. The suspensions were left undisturbed for 48 h at room temperature, and the sedimentation or flotation was observed visually at 1 h, 24 h, and 48 h.

sections.heading: Fabrication of NBC/bioepoxy nanocomposites
paragraphs: Different loading levels of CNC nanoparticles (1 wt%, 3 wt%, 5 wt%, and 7 wt% relative to the mass of the bioepoxy resin) and NBC nanoparticles (1 wt%, 3 wt%, 5 wt%, 7 wt%, 10 wt%, and 15 wt% relative to the mass of the bioepoxy resin) were first dispersed in methanol at a 2:1 weight ratio of methanol to nanoparticles using an ultrasonic bath for 1 h. Methanol was used to disrupt the van der Waals forces between the nanoparticles and achieve good dispersion. The nanoparticle/methanol mixture was then magnetically stirred and the IB2 Bio Epoxy was added. The nanoparticle/methanol/bioepoxy mixture was magnetically stirred for 5 h at 70 °C. The mixture was then stored in a vacuum oven at 50 °C for 2 days. Residual methanol was removed using a rotary evaporator at 50 °C for 1 h. To ensure that the methanol was completely removed, the total weight of the round bottom flask, magnetic stirrer, nanoparticles, and bioepoxy added was recorded and compared to the final weight of the round bottom flask containing the nanoparticle/bioepoxy mixture and if the weight was higher, additional evaporation was carried out using the rotary evaporator until the weights matched.

All samples were prepared using the resin casting method. First, three coats of Easy-Lease release agent were applied to the moulds to facilitate easy removal of the samples. The nanoparticle/bioepoxy mixture was then homogenised using a D-130 high speed homogeniser operating at 19,000 rpm for 2 min. The required amount of hardener was added (at an epoxy-to-hardener weight ratio of 100:22) to the homogenised mixture with overhead stirring at 300 rpm for 45 s. The NBC/bioepoxy mixture was carefully poured into the moulds for tensile, fracture and DMA testing, and degassed for 45 min in a vacuum chamber operating at 1 mbar. Finally, the samples were cured for 16 h at room temperature then at 40 °C for 24 h.

sections.heading: Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR)
paragraphs: A Nicolet iS5 FTIR spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, United Kingdom) was used to determine the surface functional groups of the NBC and CNC. The nanoparticles were placed on an ATR module at room temperature and analysed over a wavelength range of 550 to 4000 cm −1 . Three different samples were tested, and the average was taken.

sections.heading: Rheological properties
paragraphs: The rheological properties of the nanoparticle/bioepoxy nanocomposite with and without the use of a solvent before the addition of the hardener were tested using a cylindrical rheometer (Malvern Panalytical, United Kingdom) at 24 °C. Steady-state shear viscosity was determined by testing three samples in the range from 0.1 to 100 s −1 . The storage modulus and loss modulus were determined as a function of angular frequency in the range from 0.1 to 100 rad/s from three samples. The bioepoxy was heated to 50 °C and stirred using a magnetic stirrer while the required mass fraction of nanoparticles was added. The mixture was further stirred for 5 h. The stirred mixture was homogenised at 19,000 rpm for 2 min and then degassed for 45 min. To prepare nanocomposites with solvent-assisted dispersion, the nanoparticles were first dispersed in methanol using an ultrasonic bath for 1 h. The mixture was stirred for 5 h at 70 °C, then stirred using a magnetic stirrer and left in a vacuum oven for 2 days to completely remove the methanol.

sections.heading: Tensile properties
paragraphs: The tensile tests were carried out on five samples using a Zwick/Roell universal testing machine fitted with a 50 kN load cell according to BS EN ISO 527–2:2012 standards using 1BA geometry. The crosshead speed was set at 2 mm/min, and the tests were performed at room temperature. A clip-on extensometer with a 2.5 mm gauge length was employed to measure the elongation during the test up to the failure point. For each particle loading, five specimens were tested for statistical evaluation. The Young’s modulus (E), ultimate tensile strength (UTS), elongation at break (EL), and modulus of toughness (T) were measured for all filler loadings.

sections.heading: Fracture properties
Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA)
paragraphs: Dynamic Mechanical Analysis was carried out using a Mettler Toledo DMA 1 instrument in accordance with ASTM D4065–20. Rectangular specimens with dimensions of 35 mm × 10 mm × 4 mm) and a dimensional accuracy of ± 1% were employed. The maximum strain amplitude was 1%, which was within the linear viscoelastic range of the material. The tests were conducted in dual cantilever mode at a frequency of 1 Hz. The temperature was varied from 25 °C to 150 °C at 3 °C/min. Three samples were tested, and the average was taken.

sections.heading: Size distribution
paragraphs: Figure  2  displays the histogram of the size distribution, measure by dynamic light scattering, of NBC after cryo-milling. All particles were within the 55–80 nm range, indicating that cryo-milling was an effective process to produce NBC. Fig. 2 Histogram of the size distribution of NBC after cryo-milling

sections.heading: Surface area and pore volume
paragraphs: The BET and Barrett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) pore size analyses provide essential information about the textural characteristics of the biochar samples, including specific surface area, pore volume, and average pore size, as shown in.

Table  1 . The results demonstrate that increasing the duration of ball milling increases both surface area and pore volume. This trend can be attributed to the mechanical breakdown of larger particles into smaller fragments during milling, which creates additional surface area and introduces more defects and pores within the material. The cryo-milled biochar exhibits significantly higher surface area than the Wheat Straw Pellet (WSP), primarily due to the presence of micropores with diameters less than 2 nm. These micropores contribute to the overall surface area because of their high internal surface-to-volume ratio. Table 1 Comparison of BET surface area, pore volume, and average pore size for WSP, WSP + 15 min ball mill time, and NBC Sample BET surface area (m 2 /g) Pore volume (cm 2 /g) Average pore size (nm) WSP 2.50 ± 0.60 0.0082 2.21 ± 4.03 15 min mill WSP 23.06 ± 0.02 0.049 1.96 ± 5.11 NBC 48.02 ± 0.02 0.066 1.56 ± 5.13

The enhanced surface area and microporosity of the cryo-milled biochar have important implications for nanocomposite applications. The increased surface area enhances interfacial interactions between the biochar filler and the polymer matrix, resulting in improved dispersion and stronger interphase formation. This, in turn, enhances the mechanical, and viscoelastic properties of the resulting nanocomposite. The BET and BJH plots in Fig.  3  further support these findings, with the adsorption plots and pore size distribution curves revealing the dominance of micropores in the cryo-milled biochar and mesopores in the milled WSP. The steep nitrogen uptake at low relative pressures (P/P₀ < 0.1) in the BET plot indicates microporosity, while the BJH pore size distribution confirms the presence of pores below 2 nm in the cryo-milled sample. The calculated standard deviation exceeds the mean pore size, indicating a positive skew in the pore size distribution. This statistical spread is attributed to a long tail of larger mesopores extending beyond the primary microporous peak. Fig. 3 BET adsorption and BJH pore volume and size plots for WSP, WSP + 15 min ball mill time, and NBC

sections.heading: FTIR spectra
paragraphs: WSP, NBC, and CNC were analysed using FTIR in ATR mode, and the results are shown in Fig.  4 . Transmission bands in the regions (3000–3500 cm −1 ) and (2850–2900 cm −1 ) were observed in spectra for CNCs corresponding to O–H and C-H functional groups, respectively. These bands were absent in the spectra of WSP and NBC biochar, consistent with dehydration during pyrolysis. The biochar spectra displayed a distinctive band at around 1690 cm −1  (C =O) attributed to stretching of residual ketonic groups, whereas CNCs show no absorption in this region. Biochar showed only weak bands in the aromatic region (~ 1580 cm −1 ) corresponding to aromatic structure within the carbonaceous matrix. A broad band at 1372 cm −1  was assigned to CH₃ bending vibrations. Bands observed at 1035 and 1070 cm⁻ 1 , characteristic of C–O stretching, indicated the presence of oxygen-containing functional groups (Bartoli et al.  4 ). NBC and WSP showed identical FTIR plots which indicated that there was no contamination during the ball milling process. Fig. 4 FTIR spectra of CNCs, NBC and WSP across wavenumber ranging from 550 to 4000 cm −1

sections.heading: Dispersion stability
paragraphs: The dispersion stability of CNCs and NBC in solvents of different polarity were evaluated by dispersing each material in the selected solvents, as shown in Fig.  5 . Among the solvents examined, water was the most polar, followed by methanol, acetone then toluene. Fig. 5 Dispersion stability of NBC and CNCs in water (H 2 0), methanol (CH 3 OH), acetone (C 3 H 6 O), and toluene (C 6 H 5 CH 3 ) after 1 h, 24 h, and 48 h

CNCs disperse well in water but poorly in methanol, acetone, and toluene. This behaviour reflects the strong polarity dependence of CNC–solvent interactions. The CNC surface is rich in hydroxy (–OH) groups, which form extensive hydrogen-bonding networks with water molecules. In aqueous environments, these interactions, together with sulphate or carboxylate groups that may be introduced during processing, generate strong electrostatic repulsion and hydration layers. These effects prevent the CNC particles from aggregating, resulting in a stable dispersion. In contrast, methanol, although polar and capable of hydrogen bonding, has a lower dielectric constant than water and therefore does not stabilize charged or polar surfaces as effectively, leading to weaker solvation and eventual aggregation. Acetone, a polar aprotic solvent, interacts poorly with the hydroxy-rich surface of CNCs, making it an ineffective dispersant. Toluene, being nonpolar and incapable of hydrogen bonding or significant dipole interactions, is incompatible with the hydrophilic CNC surface, causing aggregation and sedimentation (Johnson et al.  22 ). Overall, water is the most effective solvent for dispersing CNCs due to its strong hydrogen bonding ability, high polarity, and capacity to stabilize both neutral and charged cellulose surfaces.

NBC contains various functional groups that impart amphiphilic character (Liang et al.  26 ), enabling good initial dispersion across all the solvents evaluated. In polar solvents, water, acetone, and methanol, the NBC remained well dispersed after 48 h reflecting strong compatibility between solvent polarity and the surface chemistry of the material. Acetone, a polar aprotic solvent, interacts well with aromatic and ketone groups through dipole–dipole and π–π interactions. Methanol, a polar protic solvent, can form hydrogen bonds with hydroxy and carboxylate groups which stabilise the dispersion through solvation and hydrogen bonding. Water, owing to its high polarity, effectively stabilised NBC dispersions via polar functional groups on the NBC. In addition, the porosity of NBC enhanced the interaction with the solvents by increasing the surface area and providing more active sites for solvent interactions. Initially, the NBC dispersed well in toluene, an aromatic nonpolar solvent, due to the π-π interactions between the solvent and the graphitic regions of charcoal (Johnson et al.  22 ). However, the particles began to settle after 1 h, indicating that although the NBC contained some nonpolar groups the interactions were not strong enough for long-term dispersion.

Although both CNCs and NBC dispersed well in distilled water, the high boiling point of water presents challenges for solvent removal during bioepoxy composite fabrication. Residual water would negatively affect the final mechanical properties of the nanocomposite, necessitating the selection of a solvent with a low boiling point. Methanol was chosen as the preferred solvent due to its boiling point of 65 °C and its ability to form hydrogen bonds with CNCs and NBC, promoting better dispersion.

sections.heading: Rheological properties
paragraphs: The nature of the dispersions of nanofillers and the extent of network formation within the polymer matrix were evaluated using a rotational rheometer. The variation of viscosity versus the shear rate was plotted for different nanoparticle loadings as shown in Fig.  6 a, b. Neat bioepoxy exhibited shear thinning behaviour at low shear rates which is typical of bioepoxy resins. This is due to the unravelling of the polymer chains in the bioepoxy resin and the increase in molecular orientation in the flow direction as the shear rate increases. Incorporation of nanoparticles led to a marked increase in viscosity. This effect arises from the high specific surface area of the nanofillers, which promotes adsorption of polymer chains onto particle surfaces, thereby restricting their mobility. Increasing nanoparticle loading further reduces the relative volume of free polymer available to facilitate flow, resulting in progressively higher viscosities. The nanocomposites that were dispersed in methanol exhibited higher viscosity consistent with better dispersion of the nanoparticles. FTIR confirms that both CNCs and NBC contain polar functional groups that can interact with polar solvents. These interactions disrupt the weak van der Waals forces between the nanoparticles. In addition, methanol molecules can shield the attractive forces between particles by surrounding them, which reduces the ability of the nanoparticles to interact and aggregate. Collectively these factors reduce interparticle attractions, promoting better dispersion. Consequently, fewer agglomerates formed, and the smaller, well-dispersed particles provided more adsorption sites for surrounding polymer chains. Fig. 6 Viscosity of the bioepoxy resin containing CNCs and NBC at different concentrations and without ( a ) and with  b  dispersion in methanol prior before curing

The CNC/bioepoxy composites that were dispersed in methanol also exhibited shear thinning behaviour. This reflects the combined effect of polymer chain disentanglement and the applied stress fracturing the CNC agglomerates causing the CNC nanorods to align along the shear direction (Nuruddin et al.  35 ). The NBC/bioepoxy and CNC/bioepoxy composites prepared without dispersion in methanol initially exhibited shear thinning at low shear rates, followed by shear thickening at higher shear rates. The shear thickening increased with nanoparticle loading. At lower shear rates, the nanoparticles formed layered structures, which causes shear thinning. As the shear rate increased, complex particle–matrix interactions, such as order–disorder transitions, hydrocluster formation, and contact-force mechanism, induced shear thickening. Beyond the critical shear rate, the layered structures collapsed, and the particles reorganised into micro-agglomerates known as hydroclusters. This behaviour is characteristic of systems containing spherical nanoparticles, in which the interactions are isotropic. The isotropic nature and uniform shape and size of the particles allow for easy formation of reversible hydroclusters, which causes the shear thickening effect (Wani et al.  43 ).

Dynamic viscoelastic measurements of the shear storage modulus (G’) and shear loss modulus (G’’) as functions of angular frequency are presented in Fig.  7 a, b, d, e. Neat bioepoxy exhibited fluid like behaviour (G’’ > G’) and both G’’ and G’ increasing with angular frequency. Contact between the plates and materials within the rheometer generated internal stresses that disrupted the nanoparticle packing structure. These stresses were gradually released during time-sweep testing, increasing the effective contact area and strengthening interactions between the nanoparticles and the bioepoxy matrix, ultimately leading to a progressive rise in G’. For the composite containing 1 wt% NBC without methanol pre-dispersion G’ and G’’ decreased owing to poor dispersion in the bioepoxy resin. However, when 1 wt% NBC was dispersed in methanol prior to being incorporated into the bioepoxy, the G’ and G’’ curves followed a similar trend to that of neat bioepoxy and exceeded those of non-dispersed NBC/bioepoxy composites. This behaviour confirms that methanol pre-dispersion leads to a more uniform NBC distribution in the bioepoxy compared with nanocomposites prepared without prior dispersion. At angular frequencies above 60 rad/s, nanocomposites with methanol pre-dispersed nanoparticles exhibited higher G” values due to improved nanoparticle dispersion and easier network formation within the bioepoxy (Yue et al.  45 ). Increasing NBC loading further elevated both G’ and G” with angular frequency. As more particles are added to the polymer, the mobility of the polymer chains is restricted, leading to a more pronounced elastic response and consequently a higher storage modulus. In addition, the high surface area of NBC and the increasing number of surrounding interphases led to greater energy dissipation through increased frictional interactions during deformation, resulting in a higher G’. The interphase region may also possess enhanced mechanical properties, contributing to increased stiffness and damping. Further, well- dispersed nanoparticles can form network structures that effectively bear a portion of the applied stress, leading to a higher overall storage modulus while also introducing more pathways for energy dissipation, thereby increasing the G’ (Shahbazi et al.  39 ). The CNC/bioepoxy nanocomposite with 3 wt% loading also exhibited a higher G’’ than the 7 wt% loading, indicating the presence of agglomerates in the 7 wt% nanocomposite. In summary, the rheological results demonstrate that both G’ and G’’ are dependent on the nature of the dispersion of nanoparticles within the bioepoxy system. Fig. 7 Shear storage modulus (G’), shear loss modulus (G’’), and tan δ of neat bioepoxy and nanocomposites without dispersion prior in methanol ( a – c ) and with dispersion in methanol  d – f  at different weight percentages

The dispersion and interfacial behaviour of NBC and CNCs in the bioepoxy differ markedly due to distinct morphologies and surface chemistries. NBC’s spherical, porous, and amphiphilic structure is highly compatible with methanol, enabling uniform dispersion and minimal agglomeration even at high loadings. Its porous architecture promotes mechanical interlocking and extensive polymer adsorption, creating large interphase regions that restrict chain mobility and improve stiffness, fracture toughness, and thermal stability.

By contrast, rod‑like CNCs with a highly hydrophilic, hydroxy-rich surface forms stiff percolation networks at low loadings via hydrogen bonding. Above 5 wt%, however, CNCs tend to re‑agglomerate despite solvent-assisted dispersion. Rod ends and agglomerates act as stress concentrators, disrupting stress transfer and reducing tensile strength and toughness at higher loading.

Both nanoparticles alter the viscoelastic and rheological behaviour of the bioepoxy. While neat bioepoxy shows shear‑thinning, nanoparticles incorporation increases viscosity through polymer adsorption. NBC’s high surface area and stable dispersion generate extensive interfacial regions that restrict polymer mobility and enhance network formation, resulting in higher storage and loss moduli than CNCs. CNC systems show improved viscoelasticity only at low loadings; agglomeration at higher concentrations limits energy dissipation and degrades rheological performance. Methanol improves dispersion in both systems, but NBC maintains elasticity and uniform stress transfer across a wider loading range, whereas CNC performance declines beyond 5 wt%.

sections.heading: Tensile properties
paragraphs: Tensile testing was conducted on neat bioepoxy and nanocomposites containing CNCs and BC to evaluate their mechanical properties. The CNC content was varied from 1 wt% to 7 wt% and NBC content from 1 wt% to 15 wt%. Figure  8  shows the stress–strain behaviour of the tested specimens. Figure  9 a–d shows the results for Young’s Modulus, Ultimate tensile strength (UTS), Elongation at break (EL), and modulus of toughness (T) of the nanocomposites against the weight percentages of the fillers. The bars represent the average of 5 samples, and the error bars the standard deviation for each weight percentage. Fig. 8 Stress–strain plot of CNC/bioepoxy and NBC/bioepoxy composites at different filler loadings Fig. 9 Young’s modulus ( a ), UTS ( b ), Elongation at break (%) ( c ), and modulus of toughness ( d ) of neat bioepoxy and NBC/bioepoxy and CNC/bioepoxy nanocomposites with their standard deviations

The Young’s modulus of neat bioepoxy (3.1 ± 0.2 GPa) increased with CNC loading, reaching a maximum of 3.5 ± 0.2 GPa at 5 wt%. This enhancement is attributed to minimal agglomeration at lower CNC loading, which enables nanoscale CNC structures to effectively interact with the surrounding polymer chains. These interactions generate interphase regions possessing intermediate properties between the CNCs and the bioepoxy matrix, thereby improving the overall stiffness.

As the CNC loading increases more interphase regions develop leading to the overall improvement in the matrix’s Young’s Modulus. However, at 7 wt% loading, agglomeration occurs, with some particle sizes exceeding twice the radius of gyration of the polymer chains. As a result, the surrounding polymer chains cannot adsorb onto the particle surfaces preventing the formation of effective interphase regions (Grant et al.  14 ). The increase of Young’s modulus over the neat bioepoxy at 7 wt% was due to some unagglomerated particles forming an interphase and the agglomerated particles taking some of the mechanical load, transferring stress away from the weaker polymer. For NBC/bioepoxy composites, the modulus increased with loading, reaching a maximum of 3.8 ± 0.3 GPa at 10 wt% followed by a slight decrease to 3.7 ± 0.2 GPa due to agglomeration Across equivalent loadings, NBC/bioepoxy composites exhibited higher moduli than CNC/bioepoxy composites.

NBC and CNC reinforce bioepoxy composites through fundamentally different mechanisms, which account for their contrasting tensile performance. NBC’s spherical morphology and highly porous structure enable extensive mechanical interlocking and polymer chain adsorption within its pores, creating large interphase regions that restrict chain mobility and enhance stiffness. Its amphiphilic surface chemistry promotes strong physical interactions with the matrix without introducing stress concentrators, allowing improvements in both modulus and tensile strength while maintaining ductility. In contrast, CNCs rely primarily on hydrogen bonding between its hydroxy-rich surface and the epoxy matrix, forming stiff percolation networks at low loadings. However, its rod-like geometry introduces stress concentration points at the ends of particles, and its strong hydrophilicity drives agglomeration at higher loadings, which disrupts uniform stress transfer and reduces tensile strength. These differences explain why NBC achieves superior reinforcement and toughness compared to CNCs, particularly at intermediate concentrations (Trinh and Mekonnen  40 ).

The quality of dispersion plays a critical role in stress transfer efficiency during tensile deformation. Well-dispersed NBC particles, aided by their spherical morphology and amphiphilic surface, create extensive interphase regions and maintain uniform load distribution throughout the matrix. This minimizes localized stress concentrations and allows efficient stress transfer from the polymer chains to the rigid filler, resulting in higher tensile strength and modulus. In contrast, CNC’s rod-like geometry and strong hydrophilicity lead to agglomeration at loadings above 5 wt%, even after solvent-assisted dispersion. These agglomerates act as weak points and disrupt the continuity of the stress transfer network, reducing ultimate tensile strength and increasing brittleness. Consequently, NBC’s superior dispersion enhances stress transfer efficiency compared to CNCs, explaining its better mechanical performance at intermediate and high loadings.

The UTS of the CNC/bioepoxy composites decreased with increasing CNC loading due to the combined effects of stress concentration sites and particles agglomerated. In contrast, the spherical shape of NBC minimises stress concentration, and its good dispersion prevents agglomeration. As a result, the UTS of NBC/bioepoxy composite increased compared to the neat bioepoxy.

For nanocomposites, it is well established that the addition of nanoparticles to polymer matrices reduces polymer chain mobility leading to reduced elongation at break (Zhang et al.  46 ). Nanocomposites containing NBC reached a maximum elongation of 4.1% at 1 wt% but remained ductile at 15 wt% loading with an elongation reaching to 2.9%. The toughness of NBC exceeded that of the neat bioepoxy.

Statistical groupings presented in Fig.  9 , highlight the significant differences between the two systems. NBC reinforces the bioepoxy without the severe embrittlement caused by CNC. While NBC leads to a statistically significant increases in modulus at 7 wt% loadings and above (labelled with groups ‘a’ and ‘ab’, distinct from the neat resin’s group ‘ d ’), CNC composites do not show the same level of improvement and suffer from a significant degradation in UTS at 7 wt% (dropping to group ‘e’). The divergence is most evident at 5 wt%, where CNC additions cause a sharp decline in both elongation at break and toughness, falling to groups c and d at just 5 wt%. In contrast, NBC composites at the same 5 wt% loading maintain elongation and toughness values (groups ‘ab’ and ‘a’), indicating that NBC enhances strength while preserving its ductility, and energy absorption capabilities.

Similar improvement in Young’s modulus was observed by Trinh and Mekonnen ( 40 ) for CNC/Epoxy bio nanocomposites. The Young’s modulus increased by 25.1% and 29.6% for 2.5 wt% and 5 wt% loadings, respectively. In addition, they observed the same reduction in elongation at break when CNCs were added to the epoxy matrix. Bartoli et al. ( 6 ) investigated epoxy composites incorporating micro sized biochar derived from CNCs. They found that the Young’s modulus remained comparable to that of the neat resin, while the UTS increased by 24.5%. Their composites exhibited substantial improvements in ductility, doubling at a 5 wt%, and a 150% increase in toughness. Although these previous studies have reported enhancements in mechanical properties, our findings demonstrate further improvements in terms of UTS, modulus, toughness, and elongation at break. Unlike Bartoli et al. ( 6 ), which observed minimal changes in stiffness, the composites in the present study show statistically significant increases in Young’s modulus, along with greater improvements in strength and toughness.

sections.heading: Fracture properties
paragraphs: The addition of nanofillers to a polymer matrix can enhance the fracture toughness through several reinforcing mechanisms. A key contributor is the formation of microcracks around the filler particles near the crack front, caused by the mismatch in mechanical properties, such as stiffness and thermal expansion, between the polymer and the fillers. These localised microcracks absorb energy, redistribute stress, blunt the crack tip, and slow crack propagation.

Nanofillers near the crack tip also act as energy sinks, redistributing stress over a wider area, thereby reducing the crack driving force. They can physically obstruct the crack, forcing it to deflect or pass through particles, which requires more energy. Microcrack formation often triggers plastic deformation in the surrounding matrix; nanofillers promote early onset and expansion of this plastic zone, further blunting the crack tip. As the concentration of nanofillers increases, more particles surround the crack front, promoting additional microcracking and energy dissipation.

Other toughening mechanisms include crack pinning, where nanofillers impede the crack tip, and crack deflection, which alters the crack path and increases the energy required for propagation. Additional mechanisms, such as particle pull-out and debonding, also contribute to energy absorption and plastic deformation. Collectively, these mechanisms significantly improve the fracture toughness of the nano-filled polymers.

Other toughening mechanisms include crack pinning, where nanofillers impede the crack tip, and crack deflection, which alters the crack path and increases the energy required for propagation. Additional mechanisms, such as particle pull-out and debonding, also contribute to energy absorption and plastic deformation. Collectively, these mechanisms significantly improve the fracture toughness of the nano-filled polymers (Wetzel et al.  44 ; Johnsen et al.  21 ).

Figure  10  illustrates the effect of filler loading on the force–deformation behaviour of bioepoxy composites. At low loadings (1–3 wt%), both CNC and NBC composites exhibit higher peak force and greater energy absorption than neat bioepoxy, indicating improved stiffness and toughness. For CNCs, the curve initially shows increased resistance, but it begins to flatten at higher loadings (5–7 wt%) due to agglomeration. In contrast, NBC maintains a steeper force–deformation curve up to 7 wt%, indicating superior reinforcement and delayed crack propagation. However, at very high NBC loadings (15 wt%), the curve shows reduced ductility and a slightly lower peak force, likely due to increased processing viscosity causing localized particles clustering. Overall, NBC delivers sustained mechanical improvements across a broad loading range, whereas CNC performance declines beyond moderate loadings. Fig. 10 Force–deformation plot of CNC and NBC bioepoxy composites at different filler loadings

NBC provides substantially greater enhancement, reaching a maximum fracture toughness of 138 ± 5 J/m 2  at 7 wt%, an increase of 72.7%. Its spherical shape, porous structure, and amphiphilic surface enable excellent dispersion and large interphase regions even at higher loadings. These features promote uniform stress transfer and activate multiple toughening mechanisms, including crack pinning and deflection. The porous structure also creates strong physical interlocking, restricting polymer chain mobility, blunting the crack tip, and slowing crack initiation. Although some clustering occurs at 15 wt%, the toughness of NBC nanocomposite remains higher than that of CNC nanocomposites at any equivalent loading.

Overall, NBC maintains better dispersion, stronger interfacial interactions, and more effective crack-arresting mechanisms across a wider range of loadings, resulting in significantly higher fracture toughness compared with CNCs.

The SEM images in Fig.  12  show the fracture surfaces of the SENB specimens for CNC and NBC bioepoxy nanocomposites at various magnifications. Compared to the neat bioepoxy, the nanocomposites exhibit rougher surfaces, reflecting the activation of multiple toughening mechanism. These mechanisms can be broadly classified as in-plane and out-of-plane processes. The neat bioepoxy (Fig.  12 A, B) shows feather markings characteristic of brittle failure (Domun et al.  11 ). Fig. 12 SEM micrographs of the fracture surface of neat bioepoxy ( A , B ), 3 wt% CNC/bioepoxy ( C , D ), 7 wt% NBC/bioepoxy ( E , F ), 7 wt% CNC/bioepoxy ( G , H ), 15 wt% CNC/bioepoxy ( I ,  J ), and agglomerate of CNCs present in the 7 wt% CNC/bioepoxy composite ( K ), and agglomerate of NBC present in the 15 wt% NBC/bioepoxy composite ( L ) at different magnification levels

In contrast, the fracture surface of the 3 wt% CNC (Fig.  12 C, D) and 7 wt% NBC (Fig.  12 E, F) bioepoxy nanocomposites show bowing lines, indicative of crack pinning. In addition, trench-like features are observed in the 3 wt% CNC specimen, suggesting localised plastic deformation. At higher CNC loading (7 wt%), particle agglomeration and voids formation are evident (Fig.  12 G, H, K), indicating inadequate dispersion of CNCs in methanol. These agglomerates cause microcracks initiation and voids growth, thereby accelerating failure. Similarly, voids and agglomerates are also observed in the 15 wt% NBC/bioepoxy composite (Fig.  12 L), consistent with the degradation in fracture performance at higher filler loading.

Semaan et al. ( 38 ) investigated CNC/epoxy composites and reported an 11% improvement in fracture toughness with the addition of 2 wt% CNCs. In our study, a maximum improvement of 37.2% in fracture toughness was achieved, attributed to methanol-assisted dispersion, which enhanced the uniform distribution of CNC particles within the bioepoxy matrix, resulting in reduced stress concentration. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this work presents the first investigation of the fracture properties of NBC/bioepoxy composites.

sections.heading: Dynamic mechanical analysis
paragraphs: The superior mechanical and viscoelastic enhancements observed in NBC-filled bioepoxy composites stem from key structural and morphological differences between NBC and CNC nanoparticles. NBC particles possesses a spherical geometry and highly porous architecture that provides a large surface area for polymer adsorption and promotes extensive interphase development. This structure enables uniform stress transfer and mechanical interlocking, while its amphiphilic surface ensures excellent dispersion in methanol and compatibility with the epoxy matrix. In contrast, CNCs exhibit a rigid, rod-like morphology with a highly hydrophilic surface rich in hydroxy groups. While this facilitates hydrogen bonding at low concentrations, it also drives strong particle–particle interactions, leading to agglomeration at higher loadings. These agglomerates act as stress concentrators and disrupt network formation, limiting improvements in stiffness and damping. Consequently, NBC’s isotropic geometry, porosity, and dispersion stability enable multiple reinforcement mechanisms such as chain immobilization and energy dissipation, resulting in greater gains in tensile strength, modulus, and storage modulus compared to CNC.

The overall performance of CNC and NBC-filled bioepoxy nanocomposites is governed by the interplay of dispersion quality, rheological behaviour, and particle–matrix interactions. NBC’s amphiphilic surface and spherical, porous morphology enable excellent dispersion in methanol, reducing agglomeration even at higher loadings. This uniform distribution promotes strong particle–matrix adhesion and extensive interphase formation, which immobilizes polymer chains and enhances stress transfer. Rheologically, NBC composites exhibit higher shear storage modulus and maintain elasticity under shear, indicating robust network structures that improve stiffness and damping. In contrast, CNC’s hydrophilic, rod-like geometry leads to strong particle–particle interactions and agglomeration beyond 3–5 wt%, despite solvent-assisted dispersion. These clusters disrupt stress transfer and increase viscosity disproportionately, limiting processability and mechanical gains. While CNC can form stiff percolation networks at low loadings, its poor dispersion and localized stress concentrations reduce fracture toughness and viscoelastic performance at higher concentrations. Thus, NBC’s superior dispersion stability, favourable rheology, and strong interfacial bonding collectively deliver greater improvements in tensile, fracture, and dynamic mechanical properties compared to CNC.

sections.heading: Environmental analysis
paragraphs: The environmental impact of producing CNCs via sulfuric acid hydrolysis is characterized by a significant trade-off between chemical toxicity and energy consumption. Standard CNC production is resource-intensive, requiring large volumes of strong acids, sodium hydroxide for neutralization, and high water usage for quenching and ultrafiltration. Although full acid recycling can mitigate chemical waste, it shifts the environmental burden to energy consumption, increasing electricity demand 14-fold due to the energy-intensive evaporation used to concentrate dilute acid streams. Consequently, CNC production remains a net carbon emitter, with Global Warming Potential (GWP) ranging from 16 kg CO 2  per kg of CNCs in standard scenarios to as high as 800 kg CO 2  in regions reliant on fossil fuels. In addition, the purification process results in substantial water loss, with water efficiency often as low as 4–5% in non-circular designs (Hao et al.  16 ).

In contrast, the production of nano biochar via pyrolysis followed by dry-ice cryomilling presents a markedly more favourable environmental profile, primarily driven by the carbon-negative nature of the pyrolysis stage. Biochar production effectively sequesters carbon that would otherwise degrade, and when coupled with technologies such as Chemical Looping Combustion (CLC) for the utilization of volatile byproducts (syngas and bio-oil), the process can achieve net negative emissions ranging from – 3.30 to − 3.66 kg CO 2  per functional unit. Unlike the CNC process, which consumes significant external energy to heat hydrolysis reactors, the pyrolysis step is exothermic and capable of generating its own heat, thereby reducing the net energy demand of the system (Mendiara et al.  30 ).

The comminution of biochar into nanoparticles via cryomilling reinforces the “green synthesis” classification of this pathway by eliminating the need for hazardous solvents and surfactants. Cryomilling utilizes extreme cold to induce brittleness in the material, suppressing recovery and recrystallization processes, which facilitates rapid grain refinement and fracture rather than plastic deformation. This mechanism significantly reduces processing time compared to room-temperature milling, potentially achieving nanometric sizes in 1 to 10 h versus 100 h, thereby optimizing electrical energy usage. Furthermore, the use of dry ice as a cryogen provides a dry, solvent-free environment that prevents the chemical contamination issues prevalent in wet milling or acid hydrolysis, resulting in a high-purity product without the need for extensive post-process purification or wastewater treatment (de Souza Zanuto et al.  9 ; Katiyar et al.  23 ).

sections.heading: Combined effect
paragraphs: The hybrid formulation, comprising optimum loadings (3 wt% CNCs and 7 wt% NBC), was selected to study the synergistic effect of mixing both nanofillers on the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of the resulting bioepoxy nanocomposite.

Combining 3 wt% CNCs with 7 wt% NBC potentially enables the activation of complementary toughening mechanisms. CNCs initiate local crack deflection, while NBC provides isotropic crack‑arresting behaviour and interphase‑driven energy dissipation, with potential of creating a synergistic hybrid system designed to outperform single‑filler composites. However, the hybrid composite exhibited a pronounced reduction in mechanical properties compared with both the neat bioepoxy and the single-filler systems (Figs.  14  and  15 ). As shown in Fig.  15 b, the neat bioepoxy exhibited a G IC  of 80 Jm −2 . Incorporation of CNCs at 3 wt% increased fracture toughness to 110 Jm −2 , while NBC at 7 wt% provided the highest enhancement of 138 Jm −2 . In contrast, the hybrid nanocomposite demonstrated a G IC  value of only 59 Jm −2 , corresponding to a 26% reduction relative to the neat resin. Fig. 14 Young’s modulus ( a ), UTS ( b ), elongation at break (%) ( c ), and modulus of toughness ( d ) of neat bioepoxy, nanocomposites containing 3 wt% CNCs, 7 wt% NBC, and the hybrid nanocomposite (3 wt% CNCs + 7 wt% NBC) Fig. 15 a  Critical stress intensity factor (K IC ) and  b  mode‑I fracture toughness (G IC ) of neat bioepoxy, nanocomposites containing 3 wt% CNCs, 7 wt% NBC, and the hybrid nanocomposite (3 wt% CNCs + 7 wt% NBC) measured using single‑edge‑notch bending (SENB)

This deterioration in fracture performance can be attributed to the disruption of effective energy‑dissipation mechanisms. CNC agglomeration restricts polymer infiltration into the porous NBC structure, reducing interphase formation and mechanical interlocking. CNC clusters act as stress concentrators that facilitate crack initiation and promote a more direct crack path, which counteracts the crack‑pinning and deflection mechanisms induced by NBC.

The hybrid composite exhibited a higher Tg of 68.36 ± 0.1 °C compared to the neat bioepoxy and the 3 wt% CNC/bioepoxy system (Fig.  16 ), indicating that the combined presence of CNCs and NBC increased polymer chain restriction relative to CNC alone. This increase suggests partial enhancement of interfacial interactions and network stiffness, likely arising from polymer adsorption onto the NBC surface and additional physical constraints introduced by CNCs. However, the Tg remained lower than that of the 7 wt% NBC system, which exhibited the highest Tg of 69.1 ± 0.1 °C, reflecting the superior ability of NBC alone to form extensive interphase regions and restrict chain mobility through its porous structure and isotropic morphology. The reduced Tg relative to the NBC‑only system indicates that CNCs disrupt the continuity of the NBC‑induced interphase, limiting its effectiveness. Fig. 16 Tensile storage modulus and tan δ cures for nanocomposites containing 3 wt% CNCs, 7 wt% NBC, and the hybrid composite (3 wt% CNCs + 7 wt% NBC)

From an environmental perspective, the development of hybrid composites diminishes the sustainability advantage of NBC, as the inclusion of CNC reintroduces chemically and energy‑intensive acid‑hydrolysis processing, partially offsetting the carbon‑negative benefits associated with nano‑biochar.
These findings suggest that combining NBC and CNC nanofillers at their optimum loadings does not yield any synergistic effects.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study systematically compared the reinforcement effects of cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) and wheat straw-derived nanobiochar (NBC) in bioepoxy composites. NBC demonstrated superior performance across all evaluated metrics. At 10 wt%, NBC increased Young’s modulus by 24.2% (3.8 ± 0.3 GPa) and improved ultimate tensile strength by 9.2% (71 ± 2 MPa). Incorporation of CNCs at 5 wt% loading increased Young’s modulus by 13.6% (3.5 ± 0.2 GPa) but reduced tensile strength at higher loadings due to agglomeration. NBC delivered a 72.7% improvement in fracture toughness (138 ± 5 J/m 2 ) at 7 wt%, compared to CNCs’ 37.2% increase (110 ± 11 J/m 2 ) at 3 wt%. Thermal analysis confirmed NBC’s superiority, raising Tg by 5.3% (69.1 ± 0.1 °C) versus CNCs’ modest 1.2% increase (66.5 ± 0.2 °C).

The evaluation of a hybrid formulation containing the optimum loading of CNCs (3 wt%) and NBC (7 wt%) to investigate any synergistic effects, revealed a reduction in fracture toughness below that of the neat resin, demonstrating that development of composites using both types of nanofillers does not improve mechanical performance. The results highlight that adverse nanoparticle interactions can negate individual toughening mechanisms.

Rheological studies revealed that NBC composites exhibited shear-thickening behaviour and a higher storage modulus at high frequencies, indicating robust network formation and better filler dispersion. In contrast, CNC composites showed shear-thinning and reduced mechanical performance at higher loadings, likely due to particle agglomeration. SEM fractography confirmed crack pinning and deflection mechanisms for both fillers, with NBC nanocomposite showing fewer voids and a more homogenous dispersion throughout the matrix.

Life-cycle comparison demonstrated that the nano-biochar pathway is the most environmentally sustainable production route. CNC manufacturing suffers from a high water footprint and a heavy reliance on toxic chemicals and grid electricity; while the biochar route leverages the intrinsic carbon sequestration of pyrolysis to create a carbon-negative process.

Overall, NBC proved to be a more effective and sustainable alternative for bioepoxy systems. NBC offers a sustainable, high-performance reinforcement for structural bioepoxy composites, combining superior mechanical, fracture, and thermal properties with eco-friendly processing. CNCs remain suitable for lightweight stiffness enhancement but is limited by agglomeration and reduced toughness at higher concentrations. Future work should focus on scalability for industrial applications to accelerate the adoption of bio-based composites in high-value sectors.
